What I learned¶

  • I learned that one screen of five numbers per company is enough to tell the story; the detail is there to check it, not to read first.
  • I learned that the ranking (Anthropic less expensive) holds on both prices in Sections 8 and 9, and that small moves in the rate close the gap to the last rounds, while the prices sought need much bigger ones.
  • I learned that the Base 2030 margin and sales-to-capital decide whether growth adds or destroys value, so they move the answer more than revenue alone.
  • I learned that probabilities matter more than I first thought: with every price inside my range of futures, shifting weight towards Bull can reach the last rounds.
  • I learned that a playground must work on copies, or one experiment quietly changes the model for everything after it.

Draft – to be rewritten in my own words.

Appendix: technical detail¶

Everything below is collapsed. Each part holds the original explanations, then every detail table and chart from its section, in the order they were computed. Click ▶ to open any item.

A1. Section 1 detail¶

Original explanations, collapsed. Cross-references such as '2.2' inside them use the original section numbering shown in each title.

1. Reported Revenue & Run-Rate

This section collects every revenue figure we have for each company, checks it, and lays it out, without doing any analysis yet. Growth rates and ratios come in Section 2, computed only from the figures loaded here.

Three different things people call "revenue"

Headlines about AI companies say "revenue" but usually mean one of three quite different measures. This model keeps them strictly apart:

Type (in revenue.csv) What it means Strength Weakness
run_rate The latest month's revenue × 12. A snapshot at one point in time. Up to date, which matters when revenue changes every month Based on one month, often chosen by the company. What counts as revenue is the company's call (for example, OpenAI's June 2025 figure excluded Microsoft licensing and one-off deals, per source OA3)
annual_revenue / half_year_revenue / quarter_revenue Revenue actually booked over a period (a full year, half-year or quarter) Counts real sales over the whole period, not just one month Always backward-looking. Here it comes from leaks or reports, not audited accounts
projection What the company expects or targets for a future year Shows management's own ambitions Not an outcome. Forecasts made at different dates don't form a single series

Gross vs net. Each revenue row also carries a revenue_basis label: gross, net or unknown. When a customer buys a model through a cloud partner (Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex, Microsoft Azure), the company can record the full sale and book the partner's cut as a cost (gross), or record only its own share (net). Per Axios (source BX1), Anthropic reports gross and OpenAI reports net, so their headline numbers are not measured the same way. Projections are labelled unknown. Section 2.4 tests how much this matters.

Why run-rate and booked revenue diverge for a fast-growing company: a year's booked revenue adds up all twelve months, most of them smaller than December. The run-rate leaving the year is December × 12, so it can sit well above the year's actual revenue with neither number being wrong. Putting the two on one line would make the business look like it jumped between them. So each type gets its own series, label and chart treatment.

Nothing in this section is audited. "Actual" here means a reported figure for a past period, as opposed to a projection. When the public S-1s arrive, these rows will be checked against audited numbers.

1.1 Load and check the revenue data

revenue.csv holds the figures; source_log.csv holds who said them. We join the two on source_id, so every revenue row carries its source name, URL, publish date and grade without retyping them.

Then we run hard checks. If any fails, the notebook stops with an error rather than quietly using bad data:

  • every revenue row points to a source that exists in the Source Log
  • every row uses one of the five allowed type labels and the unit USD_billions
  • every row has a revenue_basis of gross, net or unknown
  • every grade is A, B or C
  • no figure about the past was published before the period it describes (a run-rate for March can't be reported in February). Projections are exempt, since they are about the future by definition.
1.2 Grade audit: are the grades justified?

The hard checks confirm the data is well-formed. This step checks it is well-graded. Grades are assigned by hand when each source is logged, so we test them against the written rules in CLAUDE.md:

  • Grade A must come from the company itself. An A-grade figure cited through a news article gets flagged so we link the company's own statement instead.
  • Grade B is for the outlets named in CLAUDE.md (FT, Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, CNBC, The Information, Axios, New York Times). A relay (an aggregator, or a rewrite of another outlet's scoop) gets flagged so we cite the original.
  • Grade C rows (blogs, our own assumptions, and competitors' claims about rivals) are excluded from model inputs.

A flag is not an automatic downgrade. Regrading is a judgement call we make explicitly and record in the corrections log (1.3). The code never does it silently.

Some issues only a human can spot in the source text: a figure that is approximate ("about", "nearly"), a lower bound ("surpassed", "more than"), or one that conflicts with another source. These get a row-level flag, listed by hand in ROW_FLAGS below with the reason.

1.3 Corrections log

Every change to a Section 1 figure, citation or grade is recorded here, with the value before and after and the reason. The log lives in data/s1_corrections.csv, so the history survives even if the notebook is rewritten. When the public S-1s arrive, the changes they force will be added here too.

1.4 Revenue tables by company

The same function builds the table for both companies, so the two are laid out identically and can be compared directly. Each table lists every figure by type, with its basis (gross/net), grade, source and any review flag. Missing figures show up as gaps in 1.6.

1.5 Chart: reported run-rate and company projections
  • Solid line = reported run-rate (actual, not audited). Dashed lines = company projections of full-year revenue. Each dashed line joins projections from a single source only: forecasts made at different dates are separate lines, never chained into one.
  • Marker shape = source grade (★ A, ● B, ✕ C).
  • Booked figures (full year, half year, quarter) are left off the chart because they measure something different from run-rate. They are in the tables above.
  • The y-axis is on a log scale (explained in the note under the chart).
1.6 Gap register and key figures

What we don't have matters as much as what we do. The code below checks a fixed list of figures for both companies and marks each one found (with source) or GAP. Gaps stay gaps: we don't estimate them here. Where a later section needs one, it has to make an explicit, labelled judgement call.

It also builds s1_key_figures, the latest figure of each type per company. Later sections read this table instead of re-typing numbers. months_old is measured from AS_OF, the date this dataset was last updated.

1.7 Non-revenue figures: costs, losses, cash, commitments (stored for Section 3)

Revenue figures live in revenue.csv. Everything else a company reports about its finances (costs, losses, cash burn, cash, compute commitments, margins, IPO targets) is stored in data/financials.csv, linked to the Source Log the same way and graded the same way. Each row also has a figure_type, because the same metric can be reported (a past period), adjusted (a company's own non-GAAP definition), a projection, a commitment or a target, and those must never be mixed.

Main inputs so far:

  • Anthropic's leaked draft S-1 (Reuters AN11, FT AN13), 28–29 Sep 2026. A leaked draft reported by B-list outlets is grade B; it becomes A only when the public S-1 is filed.
  • OpenAI's 2024–25 financial statements, obtained by a blogger and independently verified by the FT (OA18), so graded B by the FT.
  • Company projections reported by The Information, the WSJ, CNBC and the FT.

This step only loads and checks them. Section 3 analyses them.

1.8 What Section 1 tells us (plain English)

What we have. 35 revenue figures from 23 sources, after a full re-sourcing pass. Six sources are now grade A (the companies' own posts), the rest grade B, and the grade audit flags none of them. Every relay (Techmeme, PYMNTS, VentureBeat, TechCrunch, Fortune) has been replaced by the original report or company statement. Three more sources (tagged Both) describe how the two companies count revenue; they feed Section 2.4.

Anthropic now has booked revenue, from its leaked draft S-1. Section 1 previously had only run-rates for Anthropic. Its draft IPO prospectus leaked on 28–29 September and was reviewed by Reuters and the FT. It gives FY2025 revenue of about $4.6B (Reuters) and Q2 2026 revenue of $11.5B (FT). Bloomberg had reported Q1 2026 at $4.73B. Reuters' "twelvefold" growth lets us derive FY2024 at about $0.38B; it is labelled derived and does not close the FY2024 gap. A separate report by The Information of $381M for 2024 agrees closely. OpenAI has FY2024 ($3.7B, from its 2024–25 statements as verified by the FT), FY2025 ($13.1B), H1 2025 ($4.3B) and Q1 2026 (about $5.7B). All of these are reported, not audited. A leaked draft is grade B; it becomes grade A only when the public S-1 is filed. The draft's cost, cash and IPO figures are stored in data/financials.csv for Section 3 (1.7).

Headline comparison, with caveats. Anthropic's latest run-rate ($65B, July 2026) is above OpenAI's ($40B, August 2026). In booked terms, OpenAI was ahead in Q1 2026 ($5.7B vs $4.73B), and Anthropic's Q2 alone ($11.5B+) was roughly double OpenAI's Q1. But:

  • the figures are for different months and quarters;
  • Anthropic counts cloud-partner sales gross and OpenAI counts them net, so the two headlines are not measured the same way (tested in Section 2.4);
  • both latest figures were given to investors in the run-up to an IPO. We treat them as "talking their book" and revisit them in Section 4.

Run-rate ≠ booked revenue, as expected. Both companies booked far less in FY2025 than the run-rate they left the year at (OpenAI $13.1B vs $20B; Anthropic $4.6B vs $9B). For fast growers that is normal, and it is why the two measures are never chained into one line.

Precision flags. Seven rows carry a flag. Three are approximate ("nearly $4.6B", "twelvefold", "about $5.7B"), and one marks the Q2 2026 figure as coming from a leaked draft. Anthropic's March 2026 run-rate stays at $19B: the Bloomberg article body says it "surpassed $19 billion"; only the headline says "nears $20B" (corrections log, item 11). OpenAI's Dec 2024 $5.5B may conflict with its CFO's later statement of about $6B for 2024.

Gaps that remain. Anthropic's FY2024 booked revenue (a derived estimate only); H1 2026 as a reported total for both (Anthropic's two quarters exist separately); OpenAI's Q2 2026; Anthropic's H1 2025.

What carries forward. revenue_model (all rows except C-grade) and s1_key_figures (the latest figure of each type per company) are the only revenue inputs Section 2 may use.

A2. Section 2 detail¶

Original explanations, collapsed. Cross-references such as '2.2' inside them use the original section numbering shown in each title.

2. Growth & Revenue Quality

Section 1 collected the numbers. This section asks two questions of them, using only the Section 1 data (plus the revenue-basis evidence in data/basis_evidence.csv):

  1. How fast is each company growing, and is that growth slowing? (2.1, 2.5)
  2. How good is the revenue number itself? Can run-rates be turned into booked revenue reliably (2.2)? Are company forecasts still believable (2.3)? Does the gross-vs-net accounting difference change who is bigger (2.4)?

Burn, gross margin and burn multiple are not here: they need new data, so they live in Section 3.

Every number below is computed from revenue_model. Outputs that are estimates are labelled "estimate (method), not reported". The section ends with s2_growth, the table later sections read instead of re-typing numbers.

2.1 Growth rates: compounded monthly growth rate (CMGR)

The problem. Our run-rate points are irregularly spaced: one month apart in some places, eleven months apart in others. A simple percentage change between two points mixes up how fast revenue grew with how long we waited between data points. An eleven-month jump will nearly always look bigger than a one-month jump, even if the pace was slower.

The fix: CMGR. The compounded monthly growth rate is the constant monthly growth that would turn the starting value into the ending value over the number of months between them:

$$\text{CMGR} = \left(\frac{\text{end value}}{\text{start value}}\right)^{1/\text{months}} - 1$$

Because it is a per-month rate, intervals of any length can be compared on the same scale. Two derived measures make it easier to read:

  • Annualised growth $= (1 + \text{CMGR})^{12} - 1$: the growth over a year if that monthly pace held. At these speeds the annual numbers get very large, which is itself a reminder that such paces can't last.
  • Doubling time $= \ln 2 / \ln(1 + \text{CMGR})$ months: how long revenue takes to double at that pace.

We compute CMGR between each pair of consecutive run-rate points for both companies with one shared function. Run-rates are a company-chosen measure (see Section 1), so these are growth rates of the reported run-rate, not of audited revenue.

2.2 From run-rate to booked revenue: test the method where we know the answer

Why we need a bridge. Valuation models run on booked revenue, but most of our data is run-rate. So we need a way to estimate a period's booked revenue from the run-rate path.

The method.

  1. Fill in a run-rate for every month between reported points (interpolation). The main method is log-linear interpolation: it assumes constant percentage growth between two points, which is what a straight line on the Section 1 log chart means. Linear interpolation (constant dollar growth) is shown alongside for comparison.
  2. Divide each month's run-rate by 12 to get that month's revenue (run-rate = monthly revenue × 12).
  3. Add up the months in the period.

Test before use. Before trusting the method anywhere we don't know the answer, we run it where we do. The first tests are the two full years where we have booked revenue for both companies: OpenAI FY2025 ($13.1B) and Anthropic FY2025 ($4.6B, from the leaked draft S-1). We report the error for each before using the method anywhere else. Then every other booked figure (half-years and quarters) becomes an extra test. The gap between estimate and reported figure tells us how far to trust the method, and whether it errs in one direction. It is the same idea as back-testing a trading rule on past data before risking money on it.

We chose log-linear before looking at the test results, so the test can't be used to pick whichever method happens to fit best.

Result of the planned tests

Result of the planned tests. The log-linear bridge comes in too low for both companies, by almost exactly the same amount: OpenAI's FY2025 is estimated at about $11.6B against $13.1B reported (−11.5%), and Anthropic's at about $4.1B against $4.6B (−11.1%). Linear interpolation is also low for both (−8.6% and −6.5%). The method gets the size right but misses in one direction. Two likely reasons:

  • Run-rate milestones are lower bounds. Companies announce them when they cross a round number ("surpassed $20B", "over $5B"), so the path we draw through them sits a little below the truth.
  • Definitions differ. OpenAI's June 2025 run-rate excluded Microsoft licensing and one-off deals (OA3); booked revenue includes everything.

That the bias is so similar for two companies with very different growth paths suggests it is systematic rather than bad luck. Two tests still aren't many, so next we run the method on every other booked figure we have.

2.3 Company projections vs what the run-rate path implies

A projection is a forecast made at one date. As real numbers arrive, it either holds up or gets overtaken. We check every projection in Section 1 against the most relevant actual data, using rules set in advance:

Target year Compared with Verdict
Already finished (2024, 2025) Reported booked revenue if we have it; otherwise the bridge estimate Beaten / missed, and by how much
Current year (2026) (a) estimated revenue booked so far this year; (b) a zero-growth floor = year-to-date estimate + the remaining months at today's run-rate, held flat Overtaken if (a) already exceeds the projection; consistent at zero growth if (b) does; otherwise, the average run-rate needed for the rest of the year
Future (2027+) Latest run-rate Overtaken if the run-rate already exceeds the target; otherwise, the annual growth needed to reach it

Required growth for future targets. A full year's revenue is roughly the run-rate in the middle of that year (exact under steady linear growth, close under steady compounding). So for a target of $X in year Y we compute the annual growth that takes today's run-rate to $X by mid-year Y, and to end of year Y as a softer bound. The mid-year convention is a judgement call, labelled as one.

These are consistency checks, not forecasts.

Cross-check: a quarter's revenue × 4 vs the reported run-rate

Cross-check: a quarter's revenue × 4 vs the reported run-rate. A quarter's booked revenue × 4 is another way to annualise revenue. It is the average run-rate across the quarter's three months, so for a steadily growing company it should be close to the run-rate in the middle month, and below any run-rate reported at or after the quarter's end. A large gap in the other direction (run-rates well above quarterly revenue × 4 at the same point in time) would suggest the run-rate figures are inflated.

For each booked quarter, the table compares quarter × 4 with the run-rates reported during the quarter and the next one reported after it. The last column asks: what monthly growth would turn quarter × 4 (centred on the middle month) into that next run-rate? If it is close to the growth we measured in 2.1, the two sets of numbers tell a consistent story.

What the cross-check shows

What the cross-check shows. For Anthropic's Q2 2026, quarter × 4 is $46B, and the run-rate reported in May (the quarter's middle month) was $47B: within about 2%. That is what we'd expect if the run-rates are honest snapshots of a fast-growing business. The July run-rate of $65B is 41% above quarter × 4, but it comes two months later. Closing that gap takes 18.9% a month, close to the 17.6% we measured for May–July in 2.1. So the gap is growth, not inflation.

In the other quarters the gap runs the opposite way to inflation:

  • Anthropic's Q1 2026 × 4 ($18.9B) is 35% above the February run-rate ($14B) and level with March ($19B).
  • Its Q2 2025 reconciles to August 2025 at only 16.7% a month, against a 29% interval CMGR.

In both cases booked revenue ran ahead of what the run-rate milestones implied, which matches 2.2's finding that run-rates are conservative. OpenAI's Q1 2026 × 4 ($22.8B) reconciles to its August $40B at 9.8% a month, close to its 9.1% interval CMGR. None of the four quarters suggests that reported run-rates overstate revenue.

2.4 Gross vs net: does the crossover survive?

The accounting question. When a customer buys Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex, who "made" the sale? Under the US revenue standard (ASC 606), a company that controls the product and sets the price is the principal: it records the full price as revenue and books the partner's cut as a cost (gross). A company acting as an agent records only its own share (net). Both are allowed; which applies depends on the contract terms. Per Axios (BX1, grade B), Anthropic reports gross and OpenAI reports net. So Anthropic's headline is inflated relative to OpenAI's by the partners' share of Anthropic's cloud-channel sales.

How big is the effect? We don't know the exact share, so we test a range of haircuts on Anthropic's latest run-rate. OpenAI's is already net, so it stays as reported.

Haircut Where it comes from Grade
0% As reported (gross) —
6% and 10% Axios: switching to net "would only amount to about a 6%–10% hit" B
15% Illustrative midpoint between the B-grade range and the C-grade claim Judgement call
27% Implied by OpenAI's memo claiming Anthropic's $30B was "closer to $22B" net: 1 − 22/30 C (competitor claim): sensitivity only, never a fact

We check two things: does Anthropic's latest run-rate still beat OpenAI's after the haircut, and when did the crossover happen on the monthly paths from 2.2? A haircut that is the same every month leaves growth rates (CMGR) unchanged, because it scales every point by the same factor. Only the level moves.

2.5 Growth decay: is growth slowing?

Every company's growth rate eventually falls; for valuation, the question is how fast. Section 5's scenarios will need a view on this, so here we only describe the trend. We don't forecast it.

The interval CMGRs in 2.1 jump around because the intervals have different lengths. For a smoother view we use the monthly run-rate path from 2.2 and compute the trailing 6-month CMGR at each month: the average monthly growth over the six months up to that point. Within a reported interval the interpolated path grows at a constant rate, so this is a time-weighted average of the interval CMGRs, not new information. We also show year-on-year growth (run-rate vs the same month a year earlier).

2.6 s2_growth: Section 2's headline outputs

Later sections read these values from s2_growth instead of re-typing them. Values are stored as numbers (rates as fractions, money in USD billions); the display below formats them. Every row says how it was derived, so an estimate can't be mistaken for a reported figure.

Leaked S-1 vs our run-rate picture

Until the end of September, everything we knew about Anthropic came from run-rate snapshots. The leaked draft S-1 gives the first booked figures from the company's own (draft) accounts. The table below lines them up against what the run-rate path alone would have told us.

What the draft S-1 confirms

What the draft S-1 confirms

  • The run-rate picture was a fair, slightly conservative guide. The run-rate bridge was 11% low on FY2025 and 4% low on Q2 2026. It never overstated.
  • The headline run-rates look like honest snapshots. Q2 2026 × 4 ($46B) is within about 2% of the $47B May run-rate, and the July $65B is explained by roughly 19% a month of further growth.
  • The hyper-growth is real in booked terms, not just in run-rate headlines. Booked revenue grew about 12× from 2024 to 2025, and Q2 2026 alone was 2.5× all of FY2025.

What it changes

  • Anthropic is no longer a run-rate-only company. Later sections can anchor on booked revenue (FY2025 $4.6B, Q2 2026 $11.5B) instead of bridge estimates. These are still grade B: a leaked draft, not audited, and not yet filed.
  • A year's revenue is much smaller than its exit run-rate. FY2025 booked revenue was only 51% of the December exit run-rate (38% in 2024, derived). A valuation quoted as a multiple of a $65B run-rate is a multiple of a snapshot, not of a year's sales. Section 9 has to keep these apart.
  • New risk and cost data now exists. Customer concentration, losses, compute commitments and cash are stored in data/financials.csv for Section 3. They are not analysed here.
  • The gross-vs-net question applies to booked revenue too. The draft S-1's figures are presumably on Anthropic's own gross basis (BX1), so the 2.4 haircuts are as relevant to $4.6B and $11.5B as to the run-rates.
2.7 What Section 2 tells us (plain English)

1. Two very different growth shapes. OpenAI has grown at a remarkably steady 8–12% a month for almost three years, which means revenue doubles roughly every 6 to 9 months. Anthropic has grown much faster from a much smaller base, and far less evenly: between 12% and 58% a month depending on the interval.

2. Growth is starting to slow, a little for OpenAI and sharply (but on thin evidence) for Anthropic. OpenAI's latest interval (9.1% a month, Dec 2025 → Aug 2026) is its slowest since 2024, down from 12.2% in H2 2025. Anthropic's spring 2026 surge (about 57% a month in March–May) fell to 17.6% a month in May–July. The trailing 6-month measure (34% a month) still contains the surge, so it overstates Anthropic's current pace. The slowdown rests on one two-month interval, so it is a signal to watch, not yet a trend. Section 5 takes this as an input; nothing here is a forecast.

3. Run-rates under-state booked revenue, by about 11% on average. The bridge was tested first on FY2025 for both companies and missed by almost the same amount for each: −11.5% for OpenAI and −11.1% for Anthropic. We then tested it on all eight booked figures we have. It came in too low in seven of the eight (average −10%, range −24% to +5%), most likely because run-rate milestones are announced as lower bounds. So: any booked revenue we estimate from run-rates is conservative and carries roughly ±11% uncertainty. Applying the bridge, each company has booked about $20B in 2026 so far (OpenAI January–August, Anthropic January–July). Anthropic's two reported 2026 quarters already add up to $16.2B, above OpenAI's estimated first half of $13.7B (error-adjusted range $13.1–18.1B). That suggests, but doesn't prove, that Anthropic booked more in H1 2026.

4. Anthropic's own forecasts are badly out of date; OpenAI's have held up. Anthropic's January 2026 forecast of $18B for 2026 has already been exceeded by revenue booked in the first seven months, and its run-rate is already above its $55B target for 2027. Its $70B target for 2028 needs only about 4% a year of further growth. OpenAI's forecasts have been accurate so far: FY2024 came in at its $3.7B projection and FY2025 within 1% of its $13B target. Its $36B for 2026 is consistent if growth continues: it needs an average run-rate of about $48B for September–December, against $40B in August growing about 9% a month. Its $350B target for 2030 needs 65–76% a year from today's $40B. That is well below today's 183% annualised pace, but it means holding very high growth for four more years at a scale no company has reached. The lesson for Section 5: management projections are not ceilings for Anthropic, and they aren't proof for OpenAI.

5. The gross-vs-net difference shrinks Anthropic's lead but doesn't reverse it. OpenAI reports net and Anthropic reports gross. At the B-grade 6–10% haircut, Anthropic's July run-rate is $58–61B, still about $19–21B above OpenAI's August $40B. Even at the C-grade 27% haircut implied by OpenAI's own memo, Anthropic is at $47.7B. What changes is the timing: with any haircut, the crossover on the monthly paths moves from April to May 2026. One caveat: we apply a haircut derived from April figures to July, and the share of Anthropic's sales going through cloud partners may have changed since.

6. The leaked S-1 backs up the run-rate picture rather than overturning it. Anthropic's Q2 2026 revenue × 4 ($46B) is within about 2% of the $47B run-rate it reported in May, the middle of that quarter. The jump to $65B in July is explained by about 19% a month of further growth. Across all four booked quarters, booked revenue never comes in below what the run-rates imply. The bigger change is in how to read the numbers: Anthropic's FY2025 booked revenue was only about half its exit run-rate, so run-rate headlines and annual revenue must never be swapped in a valuation.

What carries forward. s2_growth holds the latest growth rates, bridge estimates and their test error, and the basis-adjusted run-rates for both companies. Later sections read from it rather than re-typing numbers.

A3. Section 3 detail¶

Original explanations, collapsed. Cross-references such as '2.2' inside them use the original section numbering shown in each title.

3. Funding, Valuation, Capital Needs & Unit Economics

Sections 1–2 asked how big each company's revenue is and how fast it grows. Section 3 asks what investors have paid for that revenue, what it costs to produce, and how much more capital the business will need.

It is still sourced fact plus arithmetic. Where something will matter for the Section 5 scenarios (margins, burn, multiples), we record the observed range and leave the choice for later.

The symmetry rule. Every metric is computed with the same function for both companies. If a figure exists for one company but not the other, the other shows GAP: the metric is never dropped. C-grade figures appear only as labelled sensitivities.

New data files, all linked to the Source Log: data/funding.csv (rounds), data/financials.csv (now including OpenAI) and data/concentration.csv (customer and partner dependence).

3.1 Funding history

Kinds of transaction. Not every headline "valuation" comes from the same kind of deal:

Type What happens Cash to the company?
primary New shares sold to investors (a "round": Series E, F...) Yes
strategic A partner (cloud or chip company) invests, usually alongside a commercial deal Yes, but often tied to spending with that partner
tender Employees or early holders sell existing shares to new investors No: the money goes to the sellers
proposed round / IPO target Talks or a target price No: nobody has paid it yet

Pre-money and post-money. Pre-money is the value agreed for the company before the new cash; post-money = pre-money + new cash. A new investor's ownership = cash ÷ post-money.

What counts as capital raised. amount_counted_usd_bn only counts cash the company receives or has firmly been committed. It excludes:

  • tenders (the cash goes to the sellers);
  • amounts already folded into a later round (to avoid double counting);
  • tranches contingent on future events (e.g. $35B of Amazon's $50B commitment to OpenAI depends on an IPO or AGI).

The window starts in January 2023, so earlier money (e.g. Microsoft's 2019 and 2021 investments in OpenAI) is not in the totals.

3.2 What each price implied: valuation multiples

A valuation multiple divides a price by a measure of the business, so different-sized deals can be compared: valuation ÷ revenue = how many dollars investors paid per dollar of annual revenue. We compute two for every priced transaction, using Section 2's functions rather than re-typed numbers:

  • valuation ÷ run-rate at that date: run-rate from the log-linear monthly path (2.2). After the last reported point we use the latest reported run-rate, labelled.
  • valuation ÷ trailing-12-month booked revenue: estimated with the run-rate bridge (2.2), which tested about 11% low. A low revenue estimate means the multiple is somewhat overstated.

Why a funding-round price is not a fair value. A post-money valuation is the price of one class of shares, on one day, with its own terms, multiplied across all shares as if they were identical. They are not:

  • Liquidation preferences. Late-stage investors are often paid back first (sometimes with a guaranteed return) if the company is sold for less than expected. A share with that protection is worth more than a common share, so price per preferred share × all shares overstates what the whole company is worth.
  • Strategic investors (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia) are not only buying equity. They are buying a customer for their chips and clouds, so they can rationally pay more than a pure financial investor would.
  • Circular deals. A cloud or chip partner invests $X and the company commits to spend $Y with that partner. Part of the "investment" comes back to the investor as revenue. It is real money, but it is not independent evidence of value: the price partly reflects the partner's own sales. Examples in 3.1: Microsoft/Nvidia's $15B alongside Anthropic's $30B Azure commitment; Amazon's $25B alongside >$100B of AWS commitments; Amazon and Nvidia anchoring OpenAI's 2026 round.
  • Momentum. Rounds are priced off the last round and rival deals, not off discounted cash flows.

A DCF (Sections 6–9) asks a different question: what are the future cash flows worth today? The round price is a reference point to compare against, not an input.

Equity value vs enterprise value (EV). A valuation is an equity value: the price of the shares. Enterprise value = equity value − cash + debt (and other debt-like claims) is the value of the operating business on its own. A company holding $100B of cash is "worth" $100B more as equity than its business alone. A DCF of operating cash flows produces an EV, so to compare it with a round price (equity) later, we will need cash and debt. Those figures are mostly GAPs today (table below).

3.3 Unit economics: what it costs to earn a dollar of revenue

The income statement in five lines.

  1. Revenue (booked, from Section 1).
  2. Cost of revenue: the direct cost of serving customers. For an AI lab this is mostly inference compute: the chips and data centres that run the models for users. Gross margin = (revenue − cost of revenue) ÷ revenue.
  3. Operating expenses: R&D (including training compute for new models), sales & marketing, and general & admin. Operating margin = operating profit ÷ revenue; negative = operating loss.
  4. Net profit/loss: after interest, tax and non-cash accounting items (e.g. revaluing convertible securities).
  5. Cash burn: how much cash actually left the company. This is not the same as the loss: non-cash costs (stock-based pay, revaluations) are in the loss but not the burn, while investment in data centres can be in the burn but not the loss.

Three kinds of gross margin, never mixed. Reported/GAAP-style margins come from statements (OpenAI's cost of revenue). Adjusted margins use a company's own definition (OpenAI's "revenue minus inference costs" excludes other costs of revenue, so it differs from GAAP). Projected margins are forecasts. They sit in separate columns.

Formulas used below (all fractions of booked revenue for the same period):

Metric Formula
Compute ÷ revenue compute & infrastructure spend ÷ revenue
Cost of revenue ÷ revenue cost of revenue ÷ revenue (GAAP gross margin = 1 − this)
Operating margin −operating loss ÷ revenue
Net margin −net loss ÷ revenue
Burn ÷ revenue cash burn ÷ revenue

Not every company reports every line. OpenAI's statements give cost of revenue but no separate compute total; Anthropic's draft S-1 gives compute spend but (in what has been reported) no cost of revenue. So each shows GAP where the other has a number, and the two "cost" ratios are not comparable with each other.

Burn multiple and capital efficiency

Burn multiple = net cash burn ÷ net new ARR (annual recurring revenue added in the same period). It answers: how many dollars of cash did it take to add one dollar of annual revenue? Venture investors read it roughly as: below 1× excellent, 1–2× acceptable, above 2× worrying, and rising over time as a warning sign. That is a convention, not data. We measure "net new ARR" two ways: the change in run-rate from December to December (Section 2 path), and the change in booked revenue year on year.

Where cash burn is a GAP (Anthropic), we show an operating-loss proxy for both companies, side by side. It is labelled: an operating loss includes non-cash costs such as stock-based pay (so it overstates burn) and excludes data-centre investment (so it can understate it).

Revenue per $ of capital = revenue ÷ cumulative capital counted since 2023 (3.1): how much annual revenue each dollar raised has bought so far.

Which loss is "real"? Reconciling net loss, operating loss and adjusted profit

Headlines said Anthropic "lost $42B" in 2025 and OpenAI "lost $38.5B". Both numbers are true, and both are mostly accounting. The reconciliation below walks from net loss to operating loss for both companies with the same steps:

  1. Start from the net loss (GAAP, everything included).
  2. Add back the non-cash charge on convertible securities. When a company's value soars, financing instruments that convert into shares become more valuable, and accounting books that rise as a loss. No cash moves.
  3. Compare what is left with the operating loss (revenue minus operating costs). The residual is other non-operating items: interest income on cash, gains or losses on investments, tax. Our sources don't itemise them, so the residual is a GAP to explain later.
  4. Adjusted operating profit (what Anthropic reports for 2026 quarters) goes one step further and usually excludes stock-based compensation, a real cost to shareholders paid in shares instead of cash. It may exclude other items too; we don't know the full definition until the public S-1.

Why a DCF settles the debate. A DCF values the free cash flow a business generates: cash from operations minus investment. The non-cash convertible charge is excluded automatically (no cash moves). Stock-based pay doesn't leave as cash either, but it dilutes shareholders, so we'll treat it as a cost in Section 6. And the large data-centre commitments are counted, even though they barely show up in an operating loss. So the "real" loss for valuation purposes is neither $42B nor the adjusted profit: it is the cash.

Why adjusted figures still need scepticism. The company chooses what "adjusted" leaves out. Here it leaves out a large, recurring cost (stock-based pay), it is not audited, and the definition can change between quarters. Anthropic's first "profitable" quarter is profitable on that definition only.

3.4 Capital needs and runway

Both companies have signed multi-year contracts for compute (data centres, chips, cloud capacity) worth far more than they hold in cash. This subsection lines up commitments against cash, burn and revenue, then asks how much more capital each would need if its own projections came true.

  • Runway = cash available ÷ monthly burn: how many months the company could keep going without new money if burn stayed at today's rate. It is a snapshot, not a forecast: burn and revenue are both changing fast.
  • Cash available = last reported cash plus primary capital counted since that date (3.1). Where cash is a GAP (OpenAI), only the capital raised since the start of 2026 is counted, so its runway is a lower bound.
  • Funding gap = cumulative cash the company itself projects to burn before break-even, minus cash available. Same function for both. It uses whichever projection each company has been reported to give: OpenAI's cumulative free-cash-flow figure (July 2026 deck), or Anthropic's burn as a % of its own revenue forecasts.

Operating leverage: why fixed commitments cut both ways. A compute contract has to be paid whether customers show up or not, so it behaves like a fixed cost. Fixed costs magnify changes in revenue. An illustration with made-up round numbers: fixed costs 100 a year, variable costs 20% of revenue.

Revenue Variable costs Fixed costs Profit Margin
100 20 100 −20 −20%
150 30 100 +20 +13%
200 40 100 +60 +30%

Going from 150 to 200 (+33% revenue) triples profit; going from 150 to 100 (−33%) turns profit into a loss. That is the two-sided bet both companies have made: if revenue keeps compounding, margins expand very fast; if it stalls, losses deepen just as fast because the contracts don't shrink. Section 5 will build scenarios on exactly this.

3.5 Revenue concentration and contract risk

Revenue that depends on a few customers or partners is worth less than the same revenue spread widely: losing one relationship can remove a large slice at once. We record what is known for both companies on the same five questions. Gaps stay gaps: a missing disclosure is information too. It usually means the company hasn't had to publish it yet, and the public S-1s will have to.

  1. Top-customer share: how much revenue comes from the largest customers?
  2. Contract length: are large customers locked in, or can they leave at short notice?
  3. Customer mix: business/API versus consumer subscriptions.
  4. Compute-partner dependence: who supplies the capacity, and how much is committed to them?
  5. Distribution-partner economics: who sells the product, and what cut do they take?
3.6 Side-by-side scorecard

One table, both companies, the same rows. Each cell shows the value and its grade, or GAP. A computed cell takes the weakest grade of its inputs: a ratio of an A and a B figure is B. The numbers come from the DataFrames built above (s3_funding, multiples, s3_unit_economics, burn, capital_needs, concentration_table), not re-typed. They are saved in s3_scorecard for later sections.

3.7 Ranges for later

Section 5 will design scenarios (Dominance / Base / Commoditisation / Distress), and each needs assumptions for margins, burn and valuation multiples. Here we only record the ranges actually observed or projected, with their sources. No choices yet: picking a point in a range is a judgement call for Section 5, and it will be labelled as one.

Each row keeps actual, adjusted and projected values apart, because a range that mixes a company's hopes with its results would hide exactly what Section 5 needs to see.

3.8 What Section 3 tells us (plain English)

1. Both valuations price in years more of hyper-growth, and they look stretched in different ways.

  • Anthropic. Its last price ($965B, May 2026) was about 21× its run-rate at the time. That is the lowest multiple of any of its primary rounds since early 2025, because revenue grew faster than the price (44× at the Series E). But it is about 210× FY2025 booked revenue: almost all of Anthropic's revenue arrived in the last few months. The >$2T IPO target is about 31× today's run-rate and 43× Q2 2026 revenue × 4.
  • OpenAI. It has been priced at a steady 31–40× run-rate in every round since 2024. Its last price ($852B) was about 33× run-rate at the time and 65× FY2025 booked revenue. The $1.4T now being sought is about 36× today's run-rate and 63× Q1 2026 revenue × 4.
  • On run-rate, OpenAI is the more richly priced. On booked revenue, Anthropic is. Anthropic's revenue is also counted gross (2.4), which flatters its multiples slightly.
  • None of these is a fair value. Strategic investors (Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft, Google) who also sell compute to the company set several of the prices. Those are circular deals: real money, but not independent evidence of value.

2. OpenAI's spending looks riskier, mainly because of scale relative to revenue.

  • Commitments. OpenAI's ~$1.4T is about 35 years of its current run-rate; Anthropic's $518B is about 8.
  • Funding gap on its own projections. OpenAI's July 2026 deck projects $278B of cumulative negative free cash flow through 2030. Even after the $87B of non-contingent March 2026 money, that leaves up to about $191B to raise. That is roughly 12–21% of the company at prices between $700B and $1.4T (illustrative arithmetic).
  • Anthropic's own projections (burn ~33% of revenue in 2026, ~9% in 2027, break-even 2028) need no new capital, and it reports adjusted operating profits in 2026.
  • The flip side. OpenAI's growth has been capital-efficient on its own terms: a burn multiple of about 0.55× in 2025 ($8B burned for $14.5B of new run-rate). We can't compute Anthropic's, because its actual cash burn is a GAP.
  • Operating leverage cuts both ways. OpenAI's commitments are a much bigger bet on revenue continuing to compound.

3. The leaked S-1 confirms the growth, and it complicates the "Anthropic is already profitable" story.

  • Confirmed: revenue up about 12× in 2025, and most of the headline $42B loss is non-cash (about $34B is a convertible-instrument charge).
  • Complicated:
    • Anthropic still lost $8.06B at the operating level in 2025, about 175% of revenue, which is no better than OpenAI's −160%.
    • Compute spending was about 1.6× revenue.
    • The 2026 "profitable" quarters are profitable on an adjusted basis that excludes stock-based pay.
  • New risks the public narrative didn't have: two customers made up about a quarter of 2025 revenue, and many large customers have no long-term contracts.

4. The gaps that matter most for valuation

  • OpenAI's cash balance and both companies' debt. Without them there is no enterprise value (3.2) and OpenAI's runway is only a lower bound.
  • Anthropic's actual cash burn and cost of revenue. Its gross margin is known only as a projection, and its burn multiple can't be computed.
  • OpenAI's customer concentration and contract terms: all GAP.
  • The schedule and cancellability of each company's commitments. "Commitments" mean different things at different horizons.
  • OpenAI's $23.9B unexplained gap between net and operating loss (3.3), which points to problems in the relayed figures.

The public S-1s should close most of these.

What carries forward. s3_funding, s3_unit_economics and s3_scorecard (plus s3_ranges for Section 5).

A4. Section 4 detail¶

How statements are collected and graded
  • Window: January 2025 to today. Same mix of speaker types for both companies; a missing type is a GAP and is never filled with weaker sources.
  • Grade by original source. The speaker's own publication (company blog, regulator press release, investor's own release) = A. An executive or analyst speaking on record via a B-list outlet = B. A competitor's claim about a rival = C, whatever the outlet.
  • Quotes vs paraphrases. A quote is used only if it is under 25 words and was read on a page I actually opened (Anthropic's and SoftBank's posts, the FTC and Delaware AG releases, a syndicated copy of a Reuters story). Everything else, including all CNBC, Bloomberg and Reuters reports (which block automated reading), is a paraphrase. Long quotes were shortened to an exact fragment, never tidied.
  • Critics: company-specific sceptics (e.g. Michael Burry, Gary Marcus, Ed Zitron) are found mainly on their own X posts or blogs (grade C), so the company-specific critic slot is a GAP for both. One B-grade critic (Bill Gurley, via CNBC) talks about the sector as a whole and is recorded as "Both".
How check_claim() decides a verdict
  • Run-rate claims: compared with booked revenue for the period whose middle month is closest to the claim (within 6 months), annualised (quarter × 4, half × 2). At least 85% of the claim = supported; 60–85% = partly; below = not supported.
  • Growth claims: compared with the Section 2 run-rate path over the same window. Within 0.8–1.25× of the claim = supported; within 0.2–5× = partly.
  • "We will keep losing money": supported if the latest full-year operating loss is still positive.
  • Future profit dates: can't check yet (GAP) until the date arrives.
  • Commitments: compared with the company's own other spending figures. A claim within the total = supported; at least half = partly.
  • Valuations: the price ÷ latest run-rate, compared with multiples investors actually paid before. Within the range = supported ("in line with past prices", not "fair").
Statements recorded as paraphrases instead of quotes

The CNBC, Bloomberg and Reuters pages could not be opened, so every statement from them is a paraphrase even where the outlet printed a direct quote (e.g. Altman's "willing to run the loss", Friar's "voracious" and "public company in 2027", Amodei's "80-fold"). Two quotes were too long and are kept as exact fragments: the Series H sentence and Delaware AG Jennings' statement. Morningstar's Michael Field is a paraphrase because his two sentences are needed together and run over 25 words.

A5. Section 5 detail¶

How the scenarios are built
  • Starting point (from code): FY2026 revenue if the run-rate never grew again after its latest month: bridge estimate of revenue booked so far (2.2) plus the latest run-rate for the remaining months. It is the zero-growth floor from 2.3, so it is conservative.
  • Comparable basis: Anthropic reports gross, OpenAI net (1.1). Anthropic's start, run-rate and own forecasts are cut by the Axios high-end haircut (grade B) used in 2.2. Company forecasts with an unknown basis are assumed to follow the company's reporting basis.
  • Growth path: annual growth falls in a straight line from the 2027 value to the 2030 value. Revenue in 2030 is computed from it, so the drivers cannot contradict each other. Section 6 uses the same rule.
  • Base check: Base revenue may not sit above the company's own forecast for the same year without a stated reason. Bull may.
  • Bust: the company is sold for about 1× revenue (grade C assumption, the same for both). Section 9 tests it.
  • No valuation here. Section 5 only describes the futures; Sections 6–8 turn them into cash flows and values.
Research: what the companies themselves forecast (and what is missing)
  • OpenAI: the July 2026 deck reported by the FT (OA8) is the newest: $36B revenue in 2026, $350B in 2030, $856B of compute spending and −$278B of free cash flow over 2026–2030. Older: $280B for 2030 (OA5); profit in 2030 and a 2028 operating loss of about 75% of revenue (WSJ, BX4).
  • Anthropic: newest is Reuters (AN30, Aug 2026): $190–200B of revenue in 2028. Older: $18B (2026), $55B (2027) and up to $148B (2029), cash-flow positive in 2028 (The Information, AN7); $70B and $17B of free cash flow in 2028 (AN6); burn of 33% then 9% of revenue in 2026–27 (WSJ, BX4); about $180B of server spending to 2029 (AN31).
  • GAPs: neither company's 2030 operating margin; Anthropic's 2030 revenue. A 2030 figure from Coatue's investor deck exists, but it is an investor's estimate (not the company's), so it is not used.

A6. Section 6 detail¶

How the forecast is built
  • Pure functions: forecast(company, scenario, A) reads only its arguments, so the Playground can re-run it with a different ASSUMPTIONS dict. build_forecasts(A) runs it for every company and path scenario; bust_revenue(company, A) gives the Bust sale revenue.
  • Revenue: FY2026 = Section 5's start (zero-growth floor, net basis). Growth 2027–30 fades in a straight line from growth_2027 to growth_2030; every year's (1 + growth) is then multiplied by one factor so FY2030 equals revenue_2030 exactly. 2031–35: growth fades in a straight line to LONG_RUN_GROWTH.
  • Operating margin (changed 13 Oct): starts at each company's own latest figure for 2026 (own_margin_2026(), from projections.csv), then a straight line to op_margin_2030, then held. Same rule for both: an own operating margin first; failing that, own 2026 cash burn ÷ revenue as an approximation (grade C: burn also contains capex and leaves out non-cash costs); failing that, GAP and the old rule (straight line from FY2025's actual). Both companies now start from cash burn: Anthropic about one-third of revenue (WSJ, BX4), OpenAI $25B on $30B (The Information, OA32). The old rule gave Anthropic a 2026 margin near −140%, against its own one-third burn and its profitable Q2 2026 (AN24).
  • Tax: TAX_RATE × (operating profit − past losses used). Losses before FY2026 are ignored, and the US 80% limit on using them is ignored (both simplifications).
  • Reinvestment (changed 13 Oct): increase in revenue ÷ SALES_TO_CAPITAL (3.0, was 1.0). It covers only what the company builds or owns. The labs mostly rent compute, and the rent is already an operating cost inside the margin, so the old 1.0 counted compute twice. The table "Fix 3 check" sets cumulative reinvestment next to the companies' own compute plans and commitments (mostly rent, so they are not expected to match).
  • Not modelled: interest, share-based pay, the part of 2026 already gone (FY2026 is counted in full), revenue-share payments beyond the net-basis cut.
  • Checks (asserts): FY2026 and FY2030 revenue match s5_scenarios; final growth equals LONG_RUN_GROWTH; cumulative FCF adds up; no tax while losses are carried.

A7. Section 7 detail¶

How the values are computed
  • Pure functions: value_scenario(company, scenario, A) values one future; value_company(company, A, probs) returns the per-scenario values, the probability-weighted value and the share from the terminal value. Both read only their arguments, so the Playground can re-run them with another ASSUMPTIONS dict.
  • Mid-year discounting: a year's cash is assumed to arrive, on average, half-way through the year. For FY2026 only the part after VALUATION_DATE counts (about a quarter of the year), timed at the middle of that part. This fixes Section 6's "FY2026 counted in full" simplification for valuation.
  • Terminal value: FCF 2035 × (1 + TERMINAL_GROWTH) ÷ (rate after 2035 − TERMINAL_GROWTH), where the rate after 2035 is BASE_COST_OF_CAPITAL (the premium has faded), discounted with 2035's factor (the "forever" cash is mid-year too). An assert stops the model if the rate is not above growth (the formula would give infinity). With TV_FLOOR_AT_ZERO, a terminal value below zero is set to zero: a business still losing cash in 2035 would be closed or sold, not funded forever. Only OpenAI Bear is affected.
  • Bust: sale price = BUST_VALUE_MULTIPLE × Bust revenue (Section 6), discounted from the middle of BUST_YEAR. Losses before the sale are not counted.
  • Floor at zero (changed 13 Oct): value = max(value_raw, SCENARIO_VALUE_FLOOR). A negative value_raw means more money has to go in than ever comes out. Owners can lose what they put in, no more (limited liability), and on such a path they would stop funding or sell. value_raw stays in the tables so the hole is still visible.
  • A rate that falls after the IPO (changed 13 Oct): yearly_rate(year) = base + premium up to IPO_YEAR, then the premium fades in a straight line and is gone by PREMIUM_FADE_END. discount_factor(t) multiplies each calendar year's own factor (a year partly waited counts in part), so with one flat rate it gives exactly 1 / (1 + rate)^t, as before (checked by an assert). DISCOUNT_RATE is kept as the 2026 rate, for display.
  • Checks (asserts): rate above growth; base cost of capital within 1 point of Damodaran's tech range; value_raw = explicit + terminal; value = value_raw floored; terminal rate = base; flat-rate discounting matches the simple formula; weighted value = sum of contributions; 2035 FCF matches s6_forecasts; the change record reproduces the saved BEFORE values and ends at today's model.
Cross-check: terminal value vs an exit multiple

An exit multiple prices the company in 2035 the way similar companies are priced today: 2035 revenue × an EV/Sales multiple (enterprise value ÷ revenue). I use Damodaran's January 2026 figure for Software (System & Application), a group of large mature software companies (EXIT_EV_SALES, BX11, grade C), and the whole US market without financials as a low comparison.

My Gordon terminal values imply only a fraction of either multiple (column "implied EV/Sales" below). Two reasons: before the IPO the rate carries a 4-point premium on top of what public companies cost, and 2035 free cash flow is a thin slice of revenue in my forecasts. Today's software multiple also carries today's optimism. So the Gordon figure is the cautious one, and the gap shows how much the answer depends on the "forever" part.

Cash and debt (GAP)

These are enterprise values: the worth of the business's future cash. Owners also own the cash in the bank and owe any debt, so equity value = enterprise value + cash − debt. Cash comes from Section 3 (OpenAI's is only a lower bound); debt is not disclosed for either company (GAP). Neither is added in Section 7.

Why future fundraising is not counted twice

The negative free cash flow in the early years is exactly the money that has to be raised. Subtracting it in the present value already charges today's owners for it. New investors who put that money in at a fair price get shares worth what they pay, so I do not also subtract dilution: that would charge the same money twice. Dilution would matter only if new money came in below a fair price.

A8. Section 8 detail¶

How the comparison is built
  • Prices: latest_prices() reads s3_funding. Last round = the latest row of type primary/strategic/tender; price sought = the latest proposed round or IPO target. The headline valuation is used: post-money for closed rounds; OpenAI's $1.4T is pre-money in talks; Anthropic's IPO target is a lower bound ("more than $2T").
  • Values: the probability-weighted value and each future's value come from s7_values and s7_weighted (Section 7), not recomputed. An assert checks they still match value_company().
  • Ratio: my value ÷ price; above 1 = cheap vs my model. Closest future = the smallest gap between the price and a future's value.
  • Like for like (open): prices are equity values (they include the cash in the bank); my values are enterprise values. The table below adds cash (Section 3); debt is a GAP. Cash is not added in the main text: still my call. The floor at zero is now part of my value (Section 7, Fix 1, 13 Oct); the table also shows the value without it.
  • Words from numbers: the football-field title and the 8.2 / 8.3 text are built from s8_compare (field_title(), field_lines(), judgement_text()), so they change when the numbers do.

A9. Section 9 detail¶

How the reverse check works
  • Copies, never originals: assumptions_with(base, growth) deep-copies ASSUMPTIONS, sets BASE_COST_OF_CAPITAL (the public-company rate: the pre-IPO premium stays on top and fades after the IPO, as in Section 7) and LONG_RUN_GROWTH, then re-derives DISCOUNT_RATE and TERMINAL_GROWTH exactly as the control panel does. scen_with_base_revenue() copies s5_scenarios; probs_with_bull() copies SCENARIO_PROBS. An assert checks after all solves that the originals are unchanged.
  • Solver: solve() scans a grid for a sign change in (value − price), then brentq finds the exact root. No sign change = no answer in the range (shown as "impossible" or "no revenue works"). Each root is checked by re-valuing at it.
  • 9.1 revenue: only Base FY2030 revenue moves. Section 6 rescales 2027–2030 growth to reach it and fades to long-run growth after 2030 as before. Bust (sold on Bear revenue) and the other futures are unchanged. Search up to REV_SEARCH_CAP ($10T).
  • When more revenue helps: once margins settle, each $1 of new revenue needs 1 / SALES_TO_CAPITAL of investment and returns margin × (1 − tax) a year, so the return on new money is margin × (1 − tax) × SALES_TO_CAPITAL (column return_on_new_money). Above the rate after the IPO, growth adds value; below it, growth destroys value and no revenue reaches the price. Before 13 Oct (sales-to-capital 1.0, flat 14%) OpenAI's Base was below the line; this ties the result to two draft choices: the Base 2030 margins (Section 5) and SALES_TO_CAPITAL (Section 6).
  • 9.2 Bull probability: the extra is taken evenly from Bust, Bear and Base; a future at 0% drops out and the rest share evenly. At 100% the weighted value equals the Bull value.
  • 9.3 grid: rows are the public-company rate (BASE_COST_OF_CAPITAL, 6–16%), with the premium on top until the IPO; growth sets both TERMINAL_GROWTH and the 2031–2035 fade target (LONG_RUN_GROWTH), as the control panel derives them. The rate solve keeps growth at 4% and searches the public-company rate from growth + 0.5 points to RATE_SEARCH_MAX (40%).

A10. Section 10 detail¶

How the dashboard and playground are built
  • Dashboard: kpi_frame() reads s2_growth (run-rate, growth), s1_key_figures (run-rate month and grade), s7_weighted and s8_compare (value, prices, value ÷ price). The football field is Section 8's plot_football_field(). The verdict lines are built from s8_compare and s9_reverse.
  • Playground: playground_values(settings) takes a copy of ASSUMPTIONS via assumptions_with(base, growth) (Section 9: the "Public tech rate" slider sets BASE_COST_OF_CAPITAL with the pre-IPO premium on top until the IPO; growth sets TERMINAL_GROWTH and LONG_RUN_GROWTH), sets SALES_TO_CAPITAL on the copy, and changes Base revenue_2030 and op_margin_2030 on a copy of s5_scenarios. Weights are renormalised to sum to 1. Asserts check that it reproduces Section 8 at my settings and that no original changes.
  • Summary: summary_text() builds Section 0's text from s8_compare, s9_reverse, s5_scenarios, START_MARGINS and SCENARIO_PROBS, and replaces the placeholder at the top with update_display (display_id "summary").
